name: Villonco Realty Co. v. Bormaheco, Inc.
facts: During negotiations for land, the parties exchanged written proposals, discussed terms, and part of the price was paid. The seller argued no sale was perfected because the acceptance allegedly qualified the offer.
issue: Was there a meeting of minds on the thing and price, or was the acceptance a counteroffer?
doctrine: The Court examined the substance of the exchange and found the essential terms agreed upon. Under Arts. 1319 and 1475, acceptance must be absolute; a clarification or non-material request does not necessarily destroy acceptance if the response remains positive and unequivocal.
examUse: Identify the alleged deviation and decide whether it changes an essential term. Cite the rule first, then compare the actual offer and acceptance. Do not mechanically label every requested clarification a counteroffer.
note: Reviewer paraphrase of doctrine, not a verbatim quotation (per R01 pp. 2, 12).
ruling: The Court modified the trial court's decision and granted specific performance: the Cervantes spouses were ordered to convey the three Buendia lots to Bormaheco, which was in turn ordered to execute a registerable deed of sale in favor of Villonco Realty at P400.00 per square meter (less the P100,000 already paid), with Villonco to pay the P1,300,000 balance upon execution; Bormaheco was also ordered to pay P20,000 attorney's fees to Villonco and P42,000 commission to broker Edith Perez de Tagle, with costs against the defendants-appellants.

name: Sanchez v. Rigos
facts: Rigos signed an instrument entitled Option to Purchase land for a fixed price within a stated period. Sanchez attempted to exercise it by tendering the price; Rigos refused.
issue: Can an accepted unilateral promise be kept irrevocable even without consideration distinct from the price?
doctrine: Under Art. 1479 read with Art. 1324, a unilateral promise unsupported by distinct option consideration may be withdrawn before acceptance is communicated. But while it remains unwithdrawn, it can operate as an offer; timely acceptance before communicated withdrawal can result in a binding sale. The later en banc rule in Sanchez controls over inconsistent earlier doctrine.
examUse: Separate the validity of the option as a preparatory contract from the offer's ability to become a sale when accepted before withdrawal. Do not say "no separate consideration means no contract can ever arise."
note: Reviewer paraphrase of doctrine, not a verbatim quotation (per R01 pp. 2, 12).
ruling: The Court affirmed the judgment for Sanchez: Rigos was ordered to accept the judicially consigned P1,510 and execute the deed of conveyance, plus P200 attorney's fees and costs. The en banc Court reiterated the Atkins, Kroll doctrine - the offer remaining unwithdrawn when timely accepted ripens into a binding contract - and deemed the inconsistent Southwestern Sugar view abandoned or modified.

name: Tanay Recreation Center v. Fausto
facts: A lease included a priority right to purchase if the lessor decided to sell. The property was transferred without first giving the lessee the promised priority.
issue: What is the effect of a right of first refusal incorporated into another contract?
doctrine: The right of first refusal is a contractual right obliging the owner, upon deciding to sell, to make the first offer to the holder on the terms contemplated by the clause. Where integrated into a lease, it may be an indivisible term supported by the lease consideration.
examUse: Ask whether the owner had decided to sell, whether the right-holder received a genuine first offer, and whether the terms were sufficiently ascertainable. It is not automatically identical to an option at a pre-fixed price.
note: Reviewer paraphrase of doctrine, not a verbatim quotation (per R01 pp. 2, 12).
ruling: The petition was PARTIALLY GRANTED: the 1990 sale to Pacunayen was deemed rescinded; Fausto's heirs were ordered to recognize TRCDC's priority right to purchase on reasonable terms (remanded to the RTC to fix them); TCT No. M-35468 stays with Pacunayen unless TRCDC completes the purchase; and respondents were ordered to pay P20,000 actual damages (6% interest from complaint filing, 12% after finality) plus P10,000 attorney's fees and costs.

name: United Muslim and Christian Urban Poor Association v. BRYC-V Development Corp.
facts: A landowner issued a letter stating an intention to sell a parcel to an association that needed financing. The acquisition depended on raising funds; the association failed to acquire another portion within an extension, and the owner sold to a third party.
issue: Did the letters of intent create a reciprocal, enforceable promise to sell and buy under Art. 1479?
doctrine: The Court treated the letters as expressions of intention — not a sale, option, or binding bilateral promise. They lacked a definite commitment to sell exclusively to the association and were part of preliminary financing steps. The case also explains the distinction between contract to sell and conditional sale and why Art. 1544 does not simply apply to an unconsummated contract to sell.
examUse: Read the whole instrument, not just the heading. Look for definite object and price, a present promise to be bound, exclusivity or title reservation, and a condition triggering conveyance.
note: Reviewer paraphrase of doctrine, not a verbatim quotation (per R01 pp. 2, 12).
ruling: The petition was DENIED and the CA and RTC decisions AFFIRMED: the letters of intent were mere expressions of intention - not a sale, option, or binding bilateral promise - and UMCUPAI's failure to raise funds for Lot No. 300-C before its sale to BRYC-V could not be blamed on SFC. Costs against petitioner.

name: Cheng v. Genato
facts: Cited in the reviewer for the requisites of the double-sale rule rather than through a full fact pattern.
issue: When does the Art. 1544 priority ladder apply?
doctrine: Art. 1544 applies only where: (1) at least two valid sales cover exactly the same subject matter; (2) the buyers' interests conflict; and (3) both acquired from the same seller. Good faith is a separate and decisive inquiry at the relevant point.
examUse: For immovables, write the ladder in order — good-faith registration first; only absent inscription do possession and then oldest title matter.
note: Reviewer paraphrase of doctrine, not a verbatim quotation (per R01 pp. 2, 12).
ruling: The petition was DENIED and the CA decision AFFIRMED en toto: Cheng's complaint was dismissed, the annotations on Genato's titles cancelled, the Da Jose spouses (holders of the annotated contract to sell, first in good faith) were ordered to pay the balance with Genato ordered to execute the deed of absolute sale in their favor, Genato was ordered to return Cheng's P50,000, and Cheng was ordered to pay moral/exemplary damages and attorney's fees - the Court finding Cheng in bad faith for pursuing the deal with knowledge of the Da Jose agreement.

name: Paylago v. Jarabe
facts: Competing land claims arose from dealings involving hereditary and co-owner interests and a parcel with a history of earlier transfers.
issue: Can a party rely on a priority rule without proving the legally relevant title, authority, and good-faith facts?
doctrine: Resolving competing claims first requires determining what share the transferor could convey, the operative title, and the relevant facts concerning possession or registration. Do not jump directly to Art. 1544 without establishing its requisites.
examUse: For an immovable, write the priority ladder in order and separately analyze good faith. Check whether every buyer bought from the same seller and whether that seller had authority over the exact interest sold.
note: Reviewer paraphrase of doctrine, not a verbatim quotation (per R01 pp. 2, 12).
ruling: The appealed decision was AFFIRMED, with costs against the Paylago spouses: the Court sustained the finding that they were not purchasers in good faith - they knew and admitted in a lease that Jarabe had possessed the half-hectare since 1945 - so their later registered title could not prevail over Jarabe, the prior purchaser in continuous possession since 1938; registration without good faith is not enough under Art. 1544.

doctrine: A freeze order requires facts showing a probable connection between the specific account/property and unlawful activity; a broad list of accounts or income-versus-transactions inference is not enough where the evidentiary link is missing. The burden of proving probable cause always rests with the AMLC, never with the account owners (though the burden of evidence may shift once AMLC makes a prima facie case).
examUse: For freeze orders, analyze probable cause and the specific property-to-activity link; AMLC bears the burden. Quote: the burden of proving probable cause always rests with the AMLC.
facts: AMLC investigated alleged anomalous DBP loan accommodations to Deltaventure Resources, Inc., transactions involving DBP's Philex shares, and related transfers/sales, and sought to freeze many bank accounts as related to unlawful activity and money laundering. The CA lifted the freeze over most accounts, keeping only a Bank of Commerce account of Boerstar Corporation linked by evidence to the transactions.
issue: Whether AMLC sufficiently established probable cause to keep the freeze orders over the unfrozen accounts, and whether the burden shifted to account holders to prove legitimacy.
name: Republic v. Ongpin
ruling: The Court denied the Republic's petition and affirmed lifting the freeze over all but the demonstrably linked account, stressing that freeze and bank-inquiry orders are extraordinary remedies.

doctrine: The Sec. 9(c) confidentiality/tipping-off rule does not automatically bar AMLC from participating in prosecutions or lawfully disclosing information in its investigative/prosecutorial functions. A CTR/STR as financial intelligence must be distinguished from bank records and evidence obtainable through lawful processes.
examUse: Distinguish the covered person's tipping-off ban from AMLC's own investigative role: AMLC is not merely a repository of reports.
facts: In a criminal case over second-hand helicopters represented as brand new, the prosecution sought AMLC records and testimony on covered/suspicious transaction reports for a bank account; AMLC invoked AMLA confidentiality against disclosure.
issue: Whether AMLA Sec. 9(c) prohibited AMLC itself from disclosing covered or suspicious transaction reports in criminal proceedings.
name: Republic v. Sandiganbayan and Office of the Ombudsman
ruling: The Court rejected AMLC's blanket position: the Sec. 9(c) prohibition targets covered persons and their officers/employees to prevent tipping-off, while AMLC has separate statutory investigative and case-institution functions.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest — Republic v. Sandiganbayan and Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. Nos. 232724–27 (February 15, 2021)

doctrine: Bank secrecy yields to express statutory exceptions. An ex parte AMLA bank inquiry is valid when court-authorized because advance notice could defeat the investigation by allowing funds or evidence to be moved — but it is not a general license for unrestricted access to all accounts.
examUse: For bank inquiry, identify the legal authority and the bank-secrecy exception; explain the ex parte rationale and its statutory safeguards.
facts: The Republic, through AMLC, sought authority to inquire into a bank account during an anti-money-laundering investigation; the account holder challenged the bank-inquiry mechanism and ex parte (no prior notice) authorization as unconstitutional and violative of deposit confidentiality and due process.
issue: Whether the AMLA bank-inquiry provision and its ex parte procedure were unconstitutional or impermissibly intruded on confidentiality and due process.
name: Republic v. Eugenio, Jr.
ruling: The Court upheld the mechanism as an extraordinary provisional remedy aiding money-laundering investigation, reasoning that prior notice could frustrate the probe; the remedy must stay within statutory conditions and safeguards.

doctrine: The constitutional ban on imprisonment for debt does not invalidate B.P. Blg. 22 because the offense is the issuance of a worthless check — a public-welfare offense under the police power — rather than non-payment alone.
examUse: State the debt-versus-worthless-check distinction and cite police power. Court's key wording: The gravamen of the offense punished by BP 22 is the act of making and issuing a worthless check.
facts: Several BP 22 accused challenged the law as violating the ban on imprisonment for debt, impairing freedom of contract, denying equal protection, and suffering enactment defects.
issue: Is B.P. Blg. 22 unconstitutional because it may impose imprisonment for a check connected with a debt?
name: Lozano v. Martinez
ruling: No. The Court upheld the law: it penalizes issuing and circulating worthless checks, which affects public confidence in checks and banking — a valid police-power measure.

doctrine: An issuance falls outside B.P. Blg. 22 when the prosecution fails to establish the first element — that the check was issued to apply on account or for value. The exact transaction and evidence matter.
examUse: Idos is evidence-specific, not a blanket guarantee-check exemption: the check merely evidenced a future partnership share with no present debt or account. Court's key wording: The check was not intended to apply on account or for value.
facts: After dissolving their partnership, Idos issued postdated checks evidencing Alarilla's proportionate share, payable from future sale of goods and collection of receivables. One check was dishonored; Idos maintained it was assurance of an eventual share, not payment of a debt or existing account.
issue: Was the check issued to apply on account or for value under Sec. 1 of B.P. Blg. 22?
name: Idos v. Court of Appeals and People
ruling: No. The record showed no present debt or account due and payable for the check; the Court also found insufficient proof of actual knowledge of insufficiency and no adequate proof of notice of dishonor. Acquitted.

sourceRefs.section: Case Digest: Idos v. Court of Appeals and People

doctrine: A check issued as a guarantee or deposit is not for that reason alone outside B.P. Blg. 22; the purpose of issuance does not automatically create an exemption.
examUse: Contrast with Idos: guarantee purpose alone never exempts, but the State must still prove every element. Court's key wording: Batas Pambansa Bilang 22 applies even in cases where dishonored checks are issued merely in the form of a deposit or a guarantee.
facts: Victor Que, connected with Powerhouse Supply, Inc., argued his BP 22 checks merely guaranteed company purchases; the checks were dishonored and lower courts sustained conviction.
issue: Does issuance merely as a guarantee or security remove a check from B.P. Blg. 22?
name: Que v. People
ruling: No. The law does not distinguish payment checks from guarantee checks; reconsideration denied, conviction stood.

doctrine: A signatory is not automatically guilty because a signed check later bounces. Knowledge must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the Sec. 2 notice requirement must be satisfied before its presumption can apply.
examUse: Test knowledge and notice separately: corporate role without treasury control plus no personal notice defeats the presumption. Court's key wording: The prosecution has a duty to prove all the elements of the crime, including the acts that give rise to the prima facie presumption.
facts: Marketing employee Lina Lim Lao signed blank corporate checks as routine work; another person filled in payee and amounts. The checks bounced; she had no treasury/funding control, and the notice sent to the corporate main office was not shown personally received by her.
issue: Can an employee be convicted without proof of actual knowledge of insufficiency or actual notice of dishonor?
name: Lim Lao v. Court of Appeals and People
ruling: No. Knowledge is essential, the presumption is only prima facie and rebuttable, and corporate notice was not personal notice to her. Acquitted.

sourceRefs.section: Case Digest: Lim Lao v. Court of Appeals and People

doctrine: The prosecution must prove the evidentiary requirements for dishonor and the notice triggering the Sec. 2 presumption. Criminal acquittal does not erase the separate civil obligation to pay the debt the checks represent.
examUse: Reading Secs. 2 and 3 together: written notice of dishonor plus the 5-banking-day opportunity is required. Court's key wording: Without the written notice of dishonor, there can be no basis for establishing the presence of actual knowledge of insufficiency of funds.
facts: Evangeline Cabrera was convicted on three BP 22 counts for checks to Luis Go; on review she showed the demand letter was never formally offered and the evidence did not adequately prove actual written notice to her.
issue: Could the convictions stand without adequate proof of written notice of dishonor and the statutory chance to pay or arrange payment?
name: Cabrera v. People
ruling: No. Convictions reversed and Cabrera acquitted for failure of proof beyond reasonable doubt; her civil obligation for the checks' face value was upheld.

doctrine: B.P. Blg. 22 and estafa are separate offenses with different elements; no double jeopardy arises merely because the same act or check is involved, as long as each prosecution independently meets its legal requirements.
examUse: Estafa needs deceit + damage; BP 22 does not. Sec. 5 preserves RPC liability. Court's key wording: A single criminal act may give rise to a multiplicity of offenses.
facts: Peter Nierras bought oil products from Pilipinas Shell and issued nine checks on delivery; the account was closed and the checks bounced. He faced both BP 22 and Art. 315(2)(d) estafa cases and claimed the later estafa prosecutions were double jeopardy.
issue: May a person be prosecuted under both B.P. Blg. 22 and Art. 315(2)(d) for the same bouncing checks?
name: Nierras v. Dacuycuy
ruling: Yes. The offenses are distinct; a single act may violate both laws when both element sets are satisfied, and Sec. 5 expressly preserves RPC liability. Petition dismissed (certiorari also held an improper remedy against denial of a motion to quash).

doctrine: For doctrine recall, frame the answer around consumer vulnerability, the seller's conduct, the terms of the transaction and the statutory test under Art. 52. (Reviewer framing guidance; the reviewer states the syllabus supplies no facts or holding for this case.)
examUse: Use the assigned case to identify the exact challenged practice and how the adjudicator applied the statutory unfair/unconscionable standard.
name: Aowa Electronics v. DTI
note: Reviewer paraphrase: the syllabus names this case under Art. 52 without facts or holding, and the reviewer invents no case-specific quotation or procedural history (per R02 p. 3). Confirm the holding in the class-assigned decision.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: Case note: Aowa Electronics v. DTI

facts: DTI-NCR records showed at least 273 consumer complaints (2001-2007) against Aowa sharing a common pattern: mall customers were lured with "gifts" or raffle/contest prizes that could be claimed only upon buying allegedly high-quality but substantially priced products; the purchase condition was disclosed only after customers were inside the store surrounded ("ganged up on") by sales representatives; customers short of cash were pressed to use credit cards, withdraw from ATMs, or were even accompanied home to produce payment. DTI-NCR filed a Formal Charge for violation of Consumer Act Arts. 50 and 52; the Adjudication Officer (April 10, 2008) declared Aowa liable - ordering permanent nationwide cease-and-desist, cancellation of business-name registrations, and withholding of new registrations - and the DTI Appeals Committee and the CA (June 23, 2009) affirmed.
issue: Did the CA commit reversible error in affirming the DTI finding that Aowa's sales scheme violated Consumer Act Arts. 50 and 52?
ruling: No. The Court denied the petition and affirmed the CA: Aowa's scheme - concealment of the purchase condition, "ganging up" on customers, and high-pressure collection tactics - was a deceptive act under Art. 50 and an unfair/unconscionable practice under Art. 52, and the DTI acted within its mandate to protect consumers. Costs against Aowa.

doctrine: Connect the facts of the assigned decision to the applicable Consumer Act articles and the relevant special statute/rule. (Reviewer framing guidance; the reviewer gives no facts or holding for this case.)
examUse: Confirm the exact factual holding from the class-assigned decision. Do not extrapolate an unverified rule about every tobacco promotion from the case name alone.
name: DOH v. Philip Morris
note: Reviewer paraphrase: the syllabus names this case in connection with sales promotions without facts or holding (per R02 p. 3). Confirm the holding in the class-assigned decision.
facts: In November 2008 PMPMI applied through advertising agencies for BFAD sales-promotion permits under Consumer Act Art. 116 for its "Gear Up" and "Golden Stick" tobacco promos. BFAD inaction and verbal invocation of a DOH memorandum banning tobacco promotions followed; on January 5, 2009 BFAD formally denied the Gear Up application, ruling that as of July 1, 2008 all tobacco promotions, advertisements and sponsorships were already prohibited under RA 9211. PMPMI's administrative appeal failed, but the CA (August 26, 2011) found grave abuse of discretion, holding RA 9211 merely restricts (not bans) promotions and that jurisdiction over tobacco promotions belongs to the IAC-Tobacco.
issue: Did the CA err in holding that RA 9211 impliedly repealed DOH/BFAD's Art. 116 authority over tobacco sales promotions in favor of the IAC-Tobacco, and in finding grave abuse of discretion in DOH's total ban on tobacco promotions?
ruling: No. The Court denied DOH's petition: RA 9211 impliedly repealed DOH's Art. 116 authority over tobacco sales promotions, giving the IAC-Tobacco primary jurisdiction; DOH's construction that RA 9211 completely banned promotions was declared null and void; the CA was affirmed with the modification that PMPMI's applications were remanded to the IAC-Tobacco for appropriate action.

doctrine: Build the statutory analysis around Civil Code Arts. 1546-1547 and the relevant Consumer Act provision, identifying which warranty was alleged and whether the pattern concerned a defect, a representation, or a promised service. (Reviewer framing guidance; the reviewer fabricates no precise holding.)
examUse: Use the assigned decision to identify which warranty was alleged, whether the fact pattern concerned a defect, a representation, or a promised service, and the doctrine the professor expects.
name: De Guzman v. Toyota Cubao
note: Reviewer paraphrase: the syllabus lists this case at the Civil Code warranty cross-reference with only the case name (per R02 p. 4). Confirm the holding in the class-assigned decision.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: Case note: De Guzman v. Toyota Cubao

facts: On November 27, 1997 De Guzman bought a brand-new Toyota Hi-Lux (1996 model) from Toyota Cubao for P508,000 (P152,400 down, P355,600 balance payable in 36 months at 54% interest); the vehicle was delivered two days later. On October 18, 1998 he demanded a new replacement engine after it developed a crack traversing Marcos Highway during heavy rain, invoking implied warranty; Toyota Cubao denied coverage. He sued for damages on April 20, 1999 - about 17 months after delivery - and the RTC dismissed the complaint on prescription.
issue: Was the implied-warranty action already barred by prescription when filed about 17 months after delivery?
ruling: Yes. The Court denied the petition for violating the hierarchy of courts and, in any event, for lack of merit: the redhibitory action under Civil Code Art. 1571 prescribes in six months from delivery, and even under RA 7394 the implied warranty for new consumer products endures at most one year - both periods had lapsed when the April 1999 complaint was filed.

doctrine: The Court reiterated the two pactum commissorium elements — a pledge/mortgage securing a principal obligation and a stipulation for automatic appropriation by the creditor upon nonpayment — and held that the Memorandum of Agreement and Dacion in Payment constituted pactum commissorium and were void on that basis.
examUse: Substance prevails over the label “dacion en pago”: ask whether the debtor truly made a later voluntary transfer independent of the security, or whether the transfer was prearranged to vest collateral automatically upon default.
facts: Borrowers executed loan/security documents and later documents characterized as a dacion en pago after default. The creditor argued the arrangements were not an unlawful automatic appropriation.
issue: Did the documents constitute a prohibited pactum commissorium under Art. 2088?
name: Ong v. Roban Lending Corporation
ruling: The Memorandum of Agreement and Dacion in Payment were held to constitute pactum commissorium and were declared void.

doctrine: Dragnet clauses are capable of securing future indebtedness but are subject to strict construction. The reliance-on-the-security test examines whether the later credit was granted in reliance on the original mortgage or was treated as supported by a separate security; a new security can be evidence against extending the old mortgage to that loan.
examUse: Do not say every future debt is secured because a mortgage contains a broad clause. Compare the first mortgage, later promissory note, later collateral, wording and evidence of the lender's actual reliance.
facts: A bank sought to apply an earlier real estate mortgage's blanket clause to later credit accommodations, while the later transaction had separate documentation/security.
issue: Does the dragnet clause cover the subsequent loan?
name: Prudential Bank v. Alviar
ruling: The Court applied strict construction and the reliance-on-the-security test to determine whether the later credit was covered by the original mortgage.

doctrine: The Court upheld the after-acquired clause in the specific context of property acquired as additions/replacements in the business and expressly made subject to the lien, discussing immobilization and the parties' express treatment of the assets as subject to the real estate mortgage. Do not generalize it into a rule that every after-acquired movable automatically becomes real property.
examUse: State the exact clause; examine the nature/use of the asset, whether it replaces/adds to mortgaged property, the parties' intent, and whether third-party rights/registration issues arise.
facts: A lumber company mortgaged land, improvements and property used in the business. The deeds expressly covered replacement and subsequently acquired assets used in connection with the concession.
issue: Can after-acquired property be covered by the real estate mortgage?
name: People's Bank and Trust Co. v. Dahican Lumber Co.
ruling: The clause covering replacement and subsequently acquired business assets was upheld in its specific context.

doctrine: The Court distinguished equity of redemption from a right of redemption after a foreclosure sale. The general rule is that a post-sale right of redemption is associated with extrajudicial foreclosure; judicial foreclosure usually has no such post-confirmation redemption right unless a special statute grants it. Statutory bank-mortgage rights cannot be circumvented merely through assignment of the mortgage debt.
examUse: Identify the foreclosure type, whether sale is confirmed/registered, the mortgagee's status and any banking-law exception. Never use “equity” and “right” of redemption interchangeably.
facts: The dispute involved a mortgaged property and a claim to redeem after foreclosure, including the effect of assignment of the mortgage debt to an entity that was not itself a bank.
issue: When does the right of redemption exist, and is it the same as equity of redemption?
name: Huerta Alba Resort, Inc. v. Court of Appeals
ruling: Equity of redemption was distinguished from a post-sale right of redemption; assignment of the mortgage debt to a non-bank did not circumvent the statutory bank-mortgage redemption framework.

doctrine: Surplus from foreclosure must be returned to the mortgagor after applying the proceeds to the secured obligation and legally chargeable amounts. A failure to return the surplus is not necessarily a loan or forbearance of money; interest is governed by the applicable rules on obligations/damages and relevant jurisprudence.
examUse: Confirm the exact factual holding on surplus and interest from the class-assigned decision.
name: Spouses Suico v. Philippine National Bank
note: Reviewer paraphrase: the syllabus names this case for surplus with only a central-doctrine summary and no facts, citation, or holding detail (per R06 p. 4). Confirm the holding in the class-assigned decision.
facts: The Suico spouses mortgaged Mandaue City properties to PNB; on default PNB extrajudicially foreclosed (EJF Case No. 92-5-15), with the notice of sale stating an obligation of P1,991,770.38 as of March 10, 1992. At the October 30, 1992 auction PNB, the lone bidder, bid P8,511,000 but never delivered the bid price or the surplus to the sheriff. The RTC nullified the foreclosure over the notice discrepancy; the CA reversed, upholding the sale's validity and (on reconsideration) merely ordering PNB to pay the filing-fee deficiency.
issue: Did the notice-of-sale amount discrepancy and PNB's failure to deliver the bid price or surplus nullify the extrajudicial foreclosure sale?
ruling: No as to validity, but PNB must disgorge the surplus. The Court modified the CA: the sale stands - the amount discrepancy did not mislead bidders or sacrifice the property, and retaining the surplus does not invalidate the sale but gives the mortgagor a cause of action to recover it, the mortgagee being deemed trustee of the unconsumed balance - and directed PNB to return P2,101,185.08 to the Suicos with 6% interest from complaint filing (12% after finality until paid), costs against PNB.

doctrine: A health-care agreement can be a contract of insurance when its substance is an undertaking, for consideration, to cover loss or expenses resulting from illness or hospitalization. The nature of the promise — not only the contract's label — matters.
examUse: Do not automatically assume an HMO/health-care agreement falls outside insurance law because it is called a “health-care agreement.” Analyze the actual promise and the risk assumed.
facts: Ernani Trinos obtained a health-care agreement from Philamcare and answered “no” to an application question asking whether he or family members had previously consulted or been treated for listed medical conditions. During the coverage period, he suffered a heart attack and was hospitalized. Philamcare denied the claim, alleging concealment of prior medical conditions. His wife paid the hospital expenses and pursued reimbursement.
issue: Was the health-care agreement a contract of insurance, and could Philamcare avoid coverage based on alleged concealment?
name: Philamcare Health Systems, Inc. v. Court of Appeals
note: Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/50579. The Court also applied the rule that health-care contracts should be read liberally in favor of subscribers and that exclusionary language of doubtful meaning is construed strictly against the provider.
ruling: The Supreme Court denied Philamcare's petition and affirmed the Court of Appeals. It treated the agreement as insurance in substance because Philamcare, for a fee, undertook to cover specified medical and hospitalization expenses upon a covered event. The application answers did not justify the denial based merely on opinion/belief-type responses, and the relevant contestability periods had passed.

doctrine: A person need not always hold formal title or possession to have an insurable interest. A buyer/consignee may have one if the sale and related transaction mean the buyer would suffer loss if the goods were damaged. Under an all-risks cargo policy, proof of damage may shift the burden to the insurer to establish an exclusion.
examUse: Memorize the sequence: (1) show cargo was in good condition when coverage attached; (2) show damage/loss on arrival; (3) the insurer must prove that an exclusion applies.
facts: Choa Tiek Seng, the consignee/buyer of fishmeal shipped from Bangkok to Manila, insured the cargo under a marine “all risks” policy. When the cargo arrived, numerous bags were damaged and there was a shortage. The insurer refused to pay, arguing that no specific accidental cause had been proved and that the consignee lacked an insurable interest.
issue: Was the cargo loss covered by the “all risks” policy, and did the consignee have an insurable interest in goods in transit?
name: Filipino Merchants Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals
note: Lawphil: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri1989/nov1989/gr_85141_1989.html
ruling: The Supreme Court denied the insurer's petition and affirmed the award for the insured. It explained that an “all risks” policy covers loss from an accidental cause unless the insurer proves an applicable exclusion. The insured's initial burden was to show that the cargo was in good condition when coverage attached and that it was damaged upon unloading; the insurer then had to show that an excluded peril caused the loss. The consignee had an insurable interest because the perfected sale gave him an equitable interest in the goods in transit.

doctrine: A material fact is judged by its probable and reasonable influence on the insurer's risk assessment. Failure to disclose recent medical consultations may be material even when the applicant believes the condition is minor; the non-medical nature of the policy makes truthful health disclosures especially important.
examUse: Ask whether a reasonable insurer would probably be influenced by the fact when assessing the risk or deciding whether to inquire further — not whether the undisclosed fact caused the eventual loss.
facts: Jaime Canilang applied for non-medical life insurance shortly after consulting a doctor twice. He was diagnosed with sinus tachycardia and acute bronchitis and had been prescribed medication, but his medical declaration stated that he had not received medical attention in the prior five years and had not been treated or consulted for listed conditions. He later died, and the insurer denied the beneficiary's claim because of nondisclosure.
issue: Was the failure to disclose the recent medical consultations a material concealment allowing the insurer to rescind, even if the insured may have thought the ailments were minor?
name: Vda. de Canilang v. Court of Appeals
note: Court's key phrase: “probable and reasonable influence of the facts”. Full decision: https://lawyerly.ph/juris/view/c7a62
ruling: Yes. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision denying recovery under the policy. The undisclosed doctor visits, diagnoses, and medication were material because they could have prompted further inquiries or affected whether the insurer issued a non-medical policy or charged a higher premium. Materiality did not depend on the insured's subjective belief or on whether the concealed condition was ultimately the cause of death.

doctrine: The incontestability clause promotes stability and protects insured persons and beneficiaries from late repudiation. Insurers are expected to investigate policy issuance within the statutory period. The case involved a policy in force for more than two years before the insured died; the statutory text and the facts must be applied carefully when a question changes that timing.
examUse: Section 48 gives the insurer two years, while the insured is alive, to investigate and establish the claimed defects. An insurer cannot continue collecting premiums and later deny liability through a belated challenge after the statutory period has passed.
facts: Delia Sotero obtained a ₱100,000 life insurance policy issued on August 30, 1993 and named her niece, Cresencia Aban, as beneficiary. Sotero died on April 10, 1996, more than two years after issuance. After the claim, the insurer alleged that Sotero had not personally applied, was illiterate and sickly, and that Aban had effectively procured the policy and named herself beneficiary. The insurer denied the claim and later sued to annul or rescind the policy.
issue: Could the insurer still contest or rescind the policy on allegations of fraud, concealment, misrepresentation, or lack of insurable interest after the policy had been in force during the insured's lifetime for more than two years?
name: Manila Bankers Life Insurance Corporation v. Aban
note: Court's key phrase: “After two years, the defenses of concealment or misrepresentation, no matter how patent or well-founded, will no longer lie”. Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/18/56125
ruling: No. The Supreme Court denied the insurer's petition and affirmed the dismissal of its action. Section 48 gave the insurer two years, while the insured was alive, to investigate and establish the claimed defects.

doctrine: The comparison is not restricted to identical goods. A mark may be refused where the signs are similar and the goods or services are related so that the public may infer a business connection.
examUse: Spot Sec. 123.1(d)(iii): similar signs plus related goods or services can bar registration through likely confusion of business.
facts: IFP applied to register OK Hotdog Inasal Cheese Hotdog Flavor Mark for snack products. Mang Inasal opposed based on its earlier registered MANG INASAL mark for restaurant services, known for chicken inasal.
issue: Was the proposed snack mark similar to the earlier mark, with related goods and services, so that registration was barred by Sec. 123.1(d)(iii)?
keyPhrase: likely to cause deception or confusion
name: Mang Inasal Philippines, Inc. v. IFP Manufacturing Corp.
note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
ruling: The Court granted Mang Inasal's petition, applied the dominancy test, found INASAL dominant, and treated the goods and services as related in the circumstances, creating likely confusion of business.

doctrine: Likelihood of confusion may concern goods or business/source. The dominant feature, ordinary purchaser, relatedness of goods, and normal potential expansion of business matter; actual confusion is not required.
examUse: Frame confusion two ways (goods and business); dominant feature plus related condiments plus business-expansion inference.
facts: Barrio Fiesta applied to register PAPA BOY & DEVICE for lechon sauce. UFC opposed using its earlier PAPA and PAPA KETSARAP marks, including for catsup and related condiments.
issue: Was PAPA BOY & DEVICE confusingly similar to UFC's earlier registered PAPA KETSARAP mark for related food products under Sec. 123.1(d)?
keyPhrase: confusion of goods and of business may likely result
name: UFC Philippines, Inc. v. Barrio Fiesta Manufacturing Corp.
note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
ruling: The Court granted UFC's petition and reinstated the IPO rejection of PAPA BOY, finding PAPA dominant in both marks and catsup and lechon sauce closely related condiments; a purchaser could think PAPA BOY belonged to UFC's PAPA sauce family.

doctrine: Use the dominancy test. The Court expressly abandoned the holistic test for resemblance of marks under the IP Code.
examUse: Cite for the current test (dominancy) and the abandonment of the holistic test; compare visual, aural and connotative impressions of dominant features.
facts: The parties asserted competing KOLIN marks over electronic/electrical goods, requiring the Court to settle the proper resemblance test under the IP Code.
issue: Did the holistic test remain a proper alternative to the dominancy test for trademark resemblance?
keyPhrase: the use of the Holistic Test ... has been abandoned
name: Kolin Electronics Co., Inc. v. Kolin Philippines International, Inc.
note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
ruling: The En Banc Court held the holistic test abandoned and the dominancy test prescribed by the IP Code, comparing dominant features and visual, aural and connotative impressions.

doctrine: Sec. 123.1(e) looks to knowledge among the relevant sector of the public, including knowledge obtained through promotion; it is not limited to recognition by the public at large.
examUse: Cite for well-known marks: relevant-sector knowledge, including promotion-derived knowledge, suffices.
facts: Wilton Dy/Philites applied for PHILITES & LETTER P DEVICE for lighting products. Philips opposed, relying on its PHILIPS mark, recognized as registered and well-known in the Philippines.
issue: Was PHILITES & LETTER P DEVICE confusingly similar to PHILIPS, engaging well-known mark protection under Sec. 123?
keyPhrase: relevant sector of the public
name: Dy v. Koninklijke Philips Electronics N.V.
note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
ruling: The Court denied the petition and dismissed the PHILITES application, recognizing PHILIPS as registered and well-known and finding the applied-for sign confusingly similar for the same lighting products.

doctrine: The recurring elements are confusing similarity in the general appearance of the goods and intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor. Intent may be inferred from the circumstances.
examUse: Cite for unfair competition: total commercial presentation plus circumstances showing calculation to deceive and ride on goodwill.
facts: San Miguel Pure Foods sold PUREFOODS FIESTA HAM. Foodsphere sold CDO ham in packaging allegedly copying the earlier product's general appearance and layout.
issue: Did Foodsphere commit unfair competition by adopting likely misleading packaging, though the products bore different word marks?
keyPhrase: intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor
name: San Miguel Pure Foods Co., Inc. v. Foodsphere, Inc.
note: Reviewer paraphrase: syllabus-relevant facts, issue, ruling and doctrine only.
ruling: The Court sustained the unfair-competition finding, focusing on the total commercial presentation and circumstances supporting a calculated deception riding on established goodwill.

doctrine: A term generic or descriptive of a class of institutions is not exclusively appropriable unless secondary meaning is established by evidence.
examUse: Cite for genericity/secondary meaning only; the decision arose in the corporate-name context, not as a direct modern Sec. 165 holding.
facts: Lyceum of the Philippines sought to stop other educational institutions from using Lyceum in their corporate names.
issue: Did Lyceum exclusively own the generic/descriptive word through alleged secondary meaning?
keyPhrase: Lyceum is generic in character
name: Lyceum of the Philippines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals
note: Reviewer paraphrase; decided in the corporate-name context - use for genericity/secondary meaning, not as a direct Sec. 165 holding.
ruling: The Court denied the petition: Lyceum commonly denoted educational institutions, petitioner failed to prove sufficiently exclusive use signifying only its school, and the other names were not confusingly similar in their entirety.

doctrine: Comparative only. Use to discuss abstract business methods; Philippine analysis begins with RA 8293 Secs. 21-22.
facts: Applicants sought a U.S. patent for a commodity-market risk-hedging method.
issue: Was the business method patent-eligible, and was machine-or-transformation the exclusive U.S. test?
keyPhrase: machine-or-transformation test is not the exclusive test
name: Bilski v. Kappos
note: U.S. Supreme Court comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
ruling: The U.S. Supreme Court held machine-or-transformation not exclusive, but the hedging claims abstract and ineligible under U.S. law.

doctrine: Comparative only. Adding generic computing to an abstract business idea does not necessarily produce a technical invention under patent law.
facts: Patents claimed intermediated settlement implemented on a generic computer.
issue: Did generic computer implementation make the abstract settlement idea patent-eligible?
keyPhrase: generic computer implementation
name: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International
note: U.S. Supreme Court comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
ruling: The U.S. Supreme Court held the claims abstract; generic computer implementation supplied no sufficient inventive concept for eligibility.

doctrine: Comparative only. The Philippine statutory test remains Sec. 26 and Philippine doctrine.
facts: The dispute concerned combining an adjustable automobile pedal with an electronic sensor in light of prior art.
issue: Was the claimed combination obvious under U.S. patent law, and was the lower court's test overly rigid?
keyPhrase: flexible approach to the obviousness question
name: KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc.
note: U.S. Supreme Court comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
ruling: The U.S. Supreme Court rejected a rigid teaching-suggestion-motivation formula for a flexible obviousness inquiry; combining familiar elements by known methods may be obvious if yielding predictable results.

doctrine: Comparative only. Copyright originality is independent creation plus at least a minimal amount of creativity; it is not patent novelty.
facts: The dispute concerned a soccer team logo of simple parallel angled lines forming an arrow plus the cursive word Arrows.
issue: Did the logo show enough original creative authorship for U.S. copyright protection?
keyPhrase: some creative authorship in its delineation or form
name: Muller v. New York Arrows Soccer Team, Inc.
note: U.S. Court of Appeals comparative authority; not binding Philippine doctrine.
ruling: The court affirmed denial of copyright protection for lack of sufficient creative authorship in delineation or form.

doctrine: The decision construed PD 49, not the current RA 8293 wording, and addressed the charge-sufficiency/probable-cause stage. It does not eliminate the prosecution's trial burden.
examUse: Limit carefully: PD 49 disjunctive-reading case at the charging stage; do not overstate as current-law doctrine.
facts: Microsoft alleged Manansala distributed/sold unauthorized software copies; a test purchase and search yielded illicit copies. The criminal complaint was brought under Sec. 29 of then-applicable PD 49.
issue: Could sale/distribution of pirated software support the criminal copyright charge without proof the seller personally reproduced the copies?
keyPhrase: sale alone of pirated copies
name: Microsoft Corporation v. Manansala
note: Reviewer paraphrase: construed PD 49 at the charge/probable-cause stage; do not read as current RA 8293 wording.
ruling: The Court reversed the dismissal: PD 49's listed acts were read disjunctively where a conjunctive reading would be absurd, so unauthorized sale/distribution could be an infringing act.

citation: G.R. No. 159577, 3 May 2006, First Division (Panganiban, C.J.)
facts: Petitioner, hired as a shift engineer/foreman at respondent's plywood plant (1975-1999), claimed overtime pay plus premium pay for rest days and special holidays. The company countered he was a managerial employee: he supervised the boiler section, oversaw 19-36 workers, and recommended personnel actions on approved forms.
issue: Was petitioner a managerial employee exempt from Title I (hours of work) labor standards, and hence unentitled to overtime and premium pay?
ruling: No as a MANAGERIAL EMPLOYEE, yes as exempt. The Court held petitioner did not meet all three Rule I Sec. 2(b) tests (he was never an employer/department manager whose primary duty was management; he reported to the plant manager). But he squarely met the Rule I Sec. 2(c) MANAGERIAL STAFF test (management-related work, discretion and independent judgment, supervision of shifts/sections, within the 20% cap). Either exemption removes the worker from Title I coverage — petition denied, no OT or premium pay due, though SIL pay stood unappealed.
doctrine: Exemption from Title I labor standards turns on actual duties under Rule I Sec. 2, not job titles: failure of the managerial-employee test (Sec. 2(b)) does not save the claim if the worker qualifies as a member of the managerial staff (Sec. 2(c)).
name: Penaranda v. Baganga Plywood Corp.

citation: G.R. No. 195466, 2 July 2014, Second Division (Brion, J.)
facts: Petitioner worked as a butcher (slaughterer) paid P40-50 per pig on pakyaw (task) basis. He filed money claims for holiday pay, SIL pay, and 13th-month pay; the employer denied an employment relationship, invoking the 'no employer-employee relationship for pakyaw workers' line.
issue: Is a pakyaw (task-basis) worker an employee entitled to holiday pay, service incentive leave pay, and 13th-month pay?
ruling: Yes to employment, holiday pay, and SIL — no to 13th-month pay. Pakyaw is a mode of payment (Art. 97/101), not proof of independence; control (supervision, fixed rules, regular reporting at the workplace) established employment under the four-fold test. Rules I, IV, V task-basis phrases are read with 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis; Serrano, Auto Bus, Cebu Institute) — petitioner's on-premises work with determinable hours was not field personnel, so holiday and SIL pay were due (burden of proof on the employer, unmet). 13th-month pay was denied: PD 851 Sec. 3(e) exempts task-basis workers WITHOUT a field-personnel qualifier. No 'independent contractor' finding was made.
doctrine: (1) Pakyaw/task pay neither negates employment nor, without field-personnel status, defeats holiday and SIL pay — task-basis phrases in the Rules are construed with 'field personnel' by ejusdem generis; (2) the PD 851 task-basis exemption from 13th-month pay is absolute and admits no field-personnel qualification.
name: David v. Macasio

citation: G.R. No. 156367, 16 May 2005, Second Division (Chico-Nazario, J.)
facts: Respondent, a driver-conductor paid 7% commission of gross bus revenue per trip (plus a fixed amount per bus, with some guaranteed allowance), claimed SIL pay for 3 years after separation. The company argued commission-basis drivers are not entitled to SIL.
issue: Is a commission-basis driver-conductor 'field personnel' (or otherwise excluded) and hence unentitled to service incentive leave pay?
ruling: No — SIL pay due. The driver was not field personnel: inspectors, dispatchers, depot assignments, and prescribed schedules proved supervision, with determinable hours (BWC advisory opinion quoted). Rule V Sec. 1(d)'s 'task or contract basis, purely commission basis' phrase is read with 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis); a supervised commission worker is covered. Three years of SIL were commuted to cash. (The Court also stated the SIL prescription rule — Art. 291 runs from demand/refusal — and left intact the deletion of the 13th-month award for purely-commission work.)
doctrine: (1) Non-field-personnel status — supervision plus determinable hours — keeps commission-basis workers inside SIL coverage; task/commission phrases in Rule V Sec. 1(d) are construed with 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis); (2) SIL non-use commutes to cash, including on separation.
name: Auto Bus Transport Systems, Inc. v. Bautista

citation: G.R. Nos. 92174 and 102552, 10 December 1993, Second Division (Narvasa, C.J.)
facts: Routine DOLE inspections of Boie-Takeda (medical representatives on fixed salary + commission) and Fuji Xerox (salesmen on fixed salary + commission) yielded deficiency findings for excluding commissions from 13th-month pay, affirmed by the Secretary under Revised Guidelines item 5(a) (fixed wage + commission computed on total earnings). Both employers went to the Supreme Court.
issue: Are commissions part of 'basic salary' for 13th-month pay computation, and is Revised Guidelines item 5(a)'s second paragraph valid?
ruling: No and void. Commissions are excluded from 13th-month 'basic salary': PD 851 and its 1975 Rules define basic salary to exclude earnings not integrated as part of the regular/basic salary, and the Guidelines themselves exclude 'earnings and other monetary benefits which are not part of or integrated into the regular salary.' The Court distinguished Songco (commissions are 'salary' GENERICALLY for separation-pay purposes) from 'basic salary' here, and declared item 5(a)'s second paragraph VOID for unduly expanding PD 851 beyond its letter and spirit. Inspection deficiencies were set aside.
doctrine: Commissions, though 'salary' in the generic Art. 97(f)/Songco sense, are NOT part of 'basic salary' for 13th-month pay; an implementing rule that folds them into the 13th-month base is void for exceeding the decree.
name: Boie-Takeda Chemicals, Inc. v. Dela Serna (with Phil. Fuji Xerox v. Dela Serna)

citation: G.R. No. 170734, 14 May 2008, Second Division (Tinga, J.)
facts: Seven company employees with under 12 months of service received full 13th-month pay, CBA-signing bonuses, service awards, and 1993-94 leave encashment identical to full-year employees (1992-2003 CBA). For 2003-2005 the company prorated these for short-service employees, calling the prior full payment an 'honest mistake' supported by a bare affidavit. The union grieved; voluntary arbitrators ordered restoration, affirmed by the CA.
issue: Did full payment of 13th-month/bonus/leave benefits to short-service employees ripen into non-diminishable company practice under Art. 100?
ruling: Yes — affirmed. CBA interpretation was settled by the arbitrators' finding (union's construction adopted). On practice: the company failed its burden (Art. 113(c)-style payroll proof absent); the 'mistake' defense collapsed on a bare affidavit without corroborating lapses in payroll procedure; and consistent voluntary grants over the CBA period ripened into practice — no fixed minimum number of years is required (2-, 3-, and 6-year precedents cited). Proration was ordered withdrawn.
doctrine: (1) Voluntary, consistent benefit grants ripen into company practice protected by Art. 100 — no fixed minimum duration is required; (2) the employer bears the burden of proving payment according to law, and a 'mistake' defense needs corroboration beyond a bare affidavit.
name: Arco Metal Products Co., Inc. v. SAMARM-NAFLU

citation: G.R. No. 118506, 18 April 1997, First Division (Kapunan, J.)
facts: Petitioners, hotel workers at La Campana, Cotabato City, discovered on inspection that their wages fell below minimum; the employer defended by valuing on-premises meals and lodging as deductible 'facilities.' The Labor Arbiter and NLRC credited the defense based on an accountant's certification and after-the-fact summaries.
issue: May an employer deduct meals-and-lodging values from wages as 'facilities' without proof, and when are such benefits supplements instead?
ruling: No — remanded for minimum-wage differentials. Facilities (Art. 97(f)) are deductible only on three conditions: (1) proof they are customarily furnished by the trade; (2) voluntary written acceptance by the employees; (3) fair and reasonable value. None was shown: the certification was self-serving, no payrolls/receipts supported it, values were not cost-based, and no real choice existed. Moreover the benefits were SUPPLEMENTS, not facilities — required residence/odd-hour availability served the employer's convenience (citing States Marine v. Cebu Seamen's, 7 SCRA 294: the purpose test).
doctrine: (1) Facilities are deductible from wages only upon: trade-custom proof + voluntary written acceptance + fair reasonable value; (2) facilities vs supplements turns on PURPOSE — benefits furnished for the employer's convenience are non-deductible supplements.
name: Mabeza v. NLRC

citation: G.R. No. 131247, 25 January 1999, Third Division (Panganiban, J.)
facts: The union claimed wage distortion because RA 6727's P25 increase and Cebu RTWPB WO-VI-02 raised Pay Classes 1-2 (Subic and Cebu) near or above Pay Class 3 (Cebu), while Cebu Pay Class 4 earners ended below Subic Pay Class 5 earners — invoking Art. 124 and the equal-pay principle.
issue: Does regional implementation of wage orders create Art. 124 wage distortion, and do inter-regional pay inversions violate equal pay?
ruling: No to both. Wage distortion has four elements: (1) an existing hierarchy of positions with corresponding salary rates; (2) a significant change in the salary rate of a lower pay class without a concomitant increase in higher classes; (3) elimination of the distinction embodied in the structure; (4) the same region. The petition failed element 2 as to differentials and element 4 throughout: 'establishment' (NWPC Guideline 1-1992) is a single fixed location, and RA 6727 deliberately differentiates by region — inter-regional disparity (higher-ranked Subic earners below lower-ranked Cebu earners) is the law's design under Arts. 99/122, not distortion and not an equal-pay violation.
doctrine: (1) Wage distortion requires four elements (hierarchy; lower-level jump without higher-level match; elimination of distinction; SAME region/establishment); (2) regional wage-order implementation does not itself create distortion, and inter-regional pay disparity is RA 6727's design, not an equal-pay violation.
name: Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Co.
Philippine Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Court of Appeals
citation: G.R. No. 118917, 22 December 1997 (First Division, Kapunan, J.); 347 Phil. 741
facts: Investors placed money-market funds with Premiere Financing Corporation (PFC), then accepted 13 Regent Savings Bank (RSB) certificates of time deposit (P10,000 each) instead of encashment. The Traders Royal Bank check PFC issued to fund the CTDs (P125,846.07) bounced for insufficient funds and was never replaced, so RSB cancelled the CTDs as its liabilities. After RSB was suspended and liquidated by the Monetary Board, PDIC denied the investors' insurance claims. The RTC and CA still held PDIC liable for the CTDs' face value.
issue: Is PDIC liable for certificates of time deposit that state they are insured by PDIC, where the issuing bank received no money for them?
ruling: No. The Supreme Court granted PDIC's petition, reversed the CA, and absolved PDIC from any liability: the CTDs were issued without RSB receiving any money, so no deposit under the charter ever came into existence.
doctrine: PDIC's liability for insured deposits is purely STATUTORY: it rests on the existence of a deposit (money or its equivalent RECEIVED by the bank), not on the negotiability of the certificate nor on recitals that the certificate is insured by PDIC. A holder cannot be the assignee of a deposit that was never made, and a certificate's 'insured by PDIC' print does not bind PDIC.
keyPhrase: No deposit, no insurance.
examUse: Use for any problem where the deposit never reached the bank (bounced funding check, unrecorded placement, manager pocketed the cash): PDIC pays only for money actually received by the bank in the usual course of business.

name: Central Bank of the Philippines v. Court of Appeals (Triumph Savings Bank)
citation: G.R. No. 76118, 30 March 1993 (En Banc, Bellosillo, J.)
facts: On Central Bank examination reports finding Triumph Savings Bank (TSB) insolvent with probable loss to depositors and creditors, the Monetary Board issued Resolution No. 596 (31 May 1985) closing TSB, forbidding it from doing business, placing it under receivership, and appointing a receiver. TSB sued in the RTC to annul the resolution for lack of prior notice and hearing and obtained orders restoring private management subject to comptrollership; the CA affirmed.
issue: May a Monetary Board resolution placing a bank under receivership be annulled for lack of prior notice and hearing?
ruling: No. The Supreme Court reversed the CA: prior notice and hearing are not required before closure/receivership; the MB resolution may be annulled only upon a judicial finding of arbitrariness and bad faith, and until then the bank stays under receivership.
doctrine: CLOSE NOW, HEAR LATER: closure and receivership need no prior hearing — a valid police-power measure to stop asset dissipation and bank runs — because the bank gets subsequent judicial review. Lack of prior hearing is not itself arbitrariness or bad faith; those must be proved (as in Banco Filipino, where MB reports had no sound basis for insolvency). Decided under RA 265 Sec. 29, now RA 7653 Sec. 30.
keyPhrase: Close now, hear later.
examUse: Use for any closure-validity problem: no prior hearing needed; challenger must allege and prove arbitrariness and bad faith; status quo (receivership) holds pending trial.

name: So v. Philippine Deposit Insurance Corp.
citation: G.R. No. 230020, 19 March 2018 (First Division, Tijam, J.)
facts: Peter So opened a P300,000 Special Incentive Savings Account with Cooperative Rural Bank of Bulacan in April 2013 and claimed deposit insurance after its closure. PDIC investigation traced his account to the proceeds of a terminated SISA mother account co-owned by the Reyes family and denied the claim as a product of SPLITTING of deposits; his reconsideration was denied in January 2016. He filed Rule 65 certiorari in the RTC, which dismissed for lack of jurisdiction while agreeing PDIC correctly denied the claim.
issue: Does the RTC have jurisdiction over certiorari assailing PDIC's denial of a deposit insurance claim?
ruling: No. The Supreme Court denied So's petition: PDIC is a quasi-judicial agency, so certiorari lies only with the Court of Appeals under Rule 65 Sec. 4 (and charter Sec. 5(g)/Sec. 22-then), not the RTC.
doctrine: PDIC exercises QUASI-JUDICIAL power when it investigates facts, weighs evidence, and finally grants or denies deposit insurance claims — its actions are final and executory and reviewable only for grave abuse of discretion. Hence certiorari goes EXCLUSIVELY to the Court of Appeals (Rule 65 Sec. 4; Sec. 5(g) 30-day rule; Sec. 27 TRO ban), and splitting-derived accounts are properly denied.
keyPhrase: PDIC is quasi-judicial; certiorari goes only to the CA.
examUse: Use for remedy problems (where to question a PDIC denial: CA certiorari within 30 days, never RTC) and for splitting problems (mother-account tracing defeats the claim).

name: Sps. Chugani v. Philippine Deposit Insurance Corp.
citation: G.R. No. 230037, 19 March 2018 (First Division, Tijam, J.)
facts: At the invitation of the president of Rural Bank of Mawab (Davao), Inc. (RBMI), the petitioners opened time deposits through inter-branch deposits to RBMI accounts in Metrobank and China Bank and received CTDs and official receipts. After RBMI's closure, PDIC denied their claims: the accounts were not part of RBMI's outstanding deposit liabilities, the CTDs were mere replicas of unissued forms, and the money was credited to the president's PERSONAL account. The RTC dismissed their certiorari for lack of jurisdiction; the CA affirmed.
issue: Did PDIC commit grave abuse of discretion in denying claims for time deposits evidenced by CTDs but missing from bank records?
ruling: No. The Supreme Court denied the petition and affirmed the CA: the RTC had no jurisdiction (PDIC is quasi-judicial; CA-exclusive review), and PDIC's denial was validly grounded on facts, law, and regulations.
doctrine: A deposit is LEGITIMATE only if (1) received by the bank in the usual course of business, (2) recorded in the bank's books, and (3) opened per BSP/PDIC forms (PDIC Regulatory Issuance No. 2011-02). Money diverted to an insider's personal account and evidenced by replica certificates is fictitious/fraudulent — no deposit, no insurance (citing PDIC v. CA). PDIC denials stand absent capricious, whimsical, arbitrary, or despotic exercise of judgment.
keyPhrase: Legitimate deposit: received, recorded, regular.
examUse: Use for fictitious/fraudulent-deposit problems and the three-part legitimacy test; also reinforces CA-exclusive certiorari under RA 10846 Sec. 5(g).

name: China Banking Corporation v. Ortega
facts: Vicente Acaban won a default money judgment against Bautista Logging Co., B & B Forest Development Corp., and Marino Bautista. To satisfy it, the sheriff served a notice of garnishment on China Banking Corporation covering B & B Forest's deposit. The bank's cashier, Tan Kim Liong, refused to comply, invoking RA 1405. The trial court ordered him to state whether the deposit existed and to hold it intact pending further order, on pain of arrest.
issue: Whether a banking institution may validly refuse to comply with a court process garnishing the bank deposit of a judgment debtor by invoking RA 1405.
ruling: No. The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court orders: the RA 1405 prohibition on examination of or inquiry into deposits does not preclude garnishment to satisfy a judgment. Citing the 1955 congressional deliberations (Rep. Macapagal and Rep. Ramos agreed deposits 'can be attached' in ordinary civil cases), the Court reasoned Congress never intended to let debtors evade just debts by converting assets into bank deposits.
doctrine: A peso bank deposit may be garnished to satisfy a final judgment; the incidental disclosure of the deposit's existence is not the examination, inquiry, or looking into prohibited by RA 1405.
keyPhrase: there is no real inquiry in such a case, and if the existence of the deposit is disclosed the disclosure is purely incidental to the execution process
examUse: State the rule plus the 'incidental disclosure' rationale. Pair with Salvacion: peso deposits can be garnished (Ortega); foreign currency deposits generally cannot (RA 6426, Sec. 8), subject only to Salvacion's narrow equitable inapplicability.

name: Salvacion v. Central Bank of the Philippines
facts: American tourist Greg Bartelli detained and repeatedly raped 12-year-old Karen Salvacion in February 1989, then escaped from jail. The Salvacions won civil damages (RTC Makati, Civil Case No. 89-3214) and the sheriff garnished Bartelli's China Bank dollar account. The Central Bank opposed release of the funds, invoking the FCD exemption from attachment and garnishment (Sec. 113, CB Circular No. 960, implementing PD 1246/RA 6426, Sec. 8).
issue: Whether the foreign currency deposit exemption from attachment and garnishment shields Bartelli's dollar deposit from execution of the damages judgment.
ruling: On these peculiar facts, no. The Court held Sec. 113 of CB Circular No. 960 and PD 1246 (amending RA 6426, Sec. 8) inapplicable to this case 'because of its peculiar circumstances' — applying the exemption to let a transient alien wrongdoer keep his dollars beyond a child victim's reach would defeat justice (citing Civil Code Art. 10: in doubt, right and justice prevail). Respondents were ordered to comply with the writ and release enough of the dollar deposit to satisfy the judgment. The Court did not declare Sec. 8 void.
doctrine: Foreign currency deposits are generally exempt from attachment and garnishment, but the Supreme Court will refuse to apply the exemption where it would shield wrongdoing at the expense of an innocent victim — a narrow, equity-driven inapplicability, not a general rule.
examUse: Always frame as general rule (exempt) plus narrow exception (Salvacion). Never write 'FCDs can always be garnished' — the Court stressed the peculiar circumstances and left Sec. 8 intact.

name: Joseph Victor G. Ejercito v. Sandiganbayan
facts: In the plunder prosecution of Joseph Estrada and others (Criminal Case No. 26558), the Special Prosecution Panel obtained Sandiganbayan subpoenas (January 2003) compelling Export and Industry Bank and Equitable-PCI Bank to produce trust account/SPAN 858 records, a savings account, manager's checks, and 'Jose Velarde' account statements. Petitioner JV Ejercito, in whose name some accounts stood, moved to quash, invoking RA 1405; the Sandiganbayan denied the motions (February-March 2003).
issue: Whether RA 1405 bars Sandiganbayan-ordered examination of the trust, savings, and related accounts in a plunder prosecution.
ruling: No — petition dismissed; the Sandiganbayan resolutions were upheld. Two Sec. 2 exceptions applied: (1) examination upon court order in bribery/dereliction cases — plunder is of the same class, and unexplained-wealth cases are excepted since public office is a public trust (citing PNB v. Gancayco); (2) the money deposited is the subject matter of the litigation — which reaches accounts to which allegedly ill-gotten money was transferred, not only accounts in the accused's own name (citing Union Bank v. CA).
doctrine: In plunder prosecutions, court-ordered bank inquiry falls under both the bribery/dereliction exception (plunder and unexplained wealth belong to that class) and the subject-matter exception, which extends to transferee accounts that allegedly received the tainted money.
examUse: Run the two-exception analysis: bribery/dereliction covers plunder and unexplained wealth; subject matter reaches recipient accounts. Pair with Union Bank for the 'money itself' boundary.

name: Marquez v. Desierto
facts: The Ombudsman ordered Union Bank Julia Vargas branch manager Lourdes Marquez to produce bank documents for in-camera inspection of accounts linked — through Traders Royal Bank manager's checks bought by George Trivinio — to a pending FFIB investigation of Amado Lagdameo and others for RA 3019 violations. The Ombudsman invoked RA 6770, Sec. 15(8) (power to examine and have access to bank accounts and records) and moved to cite Marquez for indirect contempt when she sought judicial clarification instead of complying.
issue: Whether the Ombudsman may compel in-camera inspection of bank accounts during an investigation as an exception to RA 1405, and whether the bank manager may be cited for contempt for refusing.
ruling: No on both counts — petition granted; the Ombudsman was ordered to cease and desist. Before in-camera inspection may be allowed, there must be a pending case before a court of competent jurisdiction; the account must be clearly identified; inspection is limited to the subject matter of that pending case; and bank personnel and the account holder must be notified to be present. Here there was only an Ombudsman investigation — 'fishing for additional evidence' — which does not suffice. RA 6770 does not place the Ombudsman on the same footing as the courts.
doctrine: The Ombudsman's investigatory and subpoena powers under RA 6770 are not an exception to RA 1405; bank inquiry requires a pending court case plus the stated safeguards (identified account, limited scope, notice to bank and holder).
examUse: Classic trap: 'the Ombudsman may look into bank deposits' is FALSE. Pair with Ejercito: courts in plunder/bribery cases may order inquiry; the Ombudsman investigating alone may not.

name: Union Bank of the Philippines v. Court of Appeals
facts: Union Bank, as collecting bank, under-encoded a P1,000,000 Allied Bank check as P1,000 at PCHC clearing, discovered the error almost a year later, and billed Allied Bank P999,000 — which refused, since the transaction had long closed and the drawer's account was insufficiently funded. Union Bank sued Allied Bank before the PCHC arbitration committee for the P999,000 plus damages (alleging violation of PCHC rules) and separately petitioned the RTC to examine Allied Account No. 0111-01854-8, claiming the money was the subject matter of the litigation.
issue: Whether the P999,000 claim makes the money in the Allied account the 'subject matter of the litigation' under RA 1405, Sec. 2.
ruling: No — petition denied. The money deposited itself must be the subject matter of the litigation. Union Bank's cause of action was Allied Bank's alleged PCHC-rule violation and consequent liability for reimbursement and damages; the account balance was not the thing in dispute but relief measured by an amount. The Court distinguished the cause of action (the legal wrong) from the subject of the action (the matter or thing with respect to which the controversy arose).
doctrine: 'Subject matter of the litigation' means the money deposited itself is the thing in dispute; a claim for reimbursement or damages merely measured by an amount does not qualify.
examUse: Apply the subject-matter vs cause-of-action distinction. Pair with Ejercito: traced tainted money in transferee accounts does qualify; an inter-bank reimbursement claim does not.

name: PDIC v. Philippine Countryside Rural Bank, Inc.
facts: Acting on BSP examination reports flagging the commonly controlled 'Legacy Banks' and on a corporate depositor's complaint against PCRBI (loans settled by dacion of already-foreclosed properties), the PDIC Board passed resolutions (2005-03-032, 2005-05-056) creating a Special Investigation Team under RA 3591, Sec. 9(b-1). The banks obtained a Court of Appeals injunction barring further PDIC investigation or examination without Monetary Board approval.
issue: Whether PDIC investigation of the banks requires prior Monetary Board approval — that is, whether the Sec. 9(b-1) investigation power is the same as the Sec. 8 examination power.
ruling: No — petition granted; the Court of Appeals decision was reversed and set aside. The Sec. 9(b-1) power to investigate is distinct from the Sec. 8 power to examine and needs no MB approval. The decision quotes the Charter's inquiry framework, including the Eighth power allowing the Corporation and/or the BSP to inquire into or examine deposit accounts and related information on a finding of unsafe or unsound banking practice, notwithstanding RA 1405, RA 6426, RA 8791, and other laws.
doctrine: PDIC's investigation power is independent of its examination power; and on a finding of unsafe or unsound banking practice, the Charter authorizes PDIC/BSP inquiry into deposit accounts despite bank-secrecy laws.
examUse: Use for two points: investigation needs no MB approval (vs examination), and the unsafe-practice finding is the trigger for lawful PDIC/BSP deposit inquiry (now RA 3591, Sec. 8 as amended by RA 11840).

name: United Coconut Planters Bank v. Spouses Samuel and Odette Beluso
citation: G.R. No. 159912, 17 August 2007 (Third Division, Chico-Nazario, J.)
facts: UCPB granted the Beluso spouses a credit line (up to P2.35M) secured by real-estate mortgage. The promissory notes let UCPB fix interest 'at the rate indicative of DBD retail rate or as determined by the Branch Head,' subject to increase at the lender's discretion. UCPB charged 18%-34% interest plus penalties; the Belusos paid P763,692.03, then sued to annul the interest stipulation, the accounting, and the foreclosure. The RTC and CA voided the interest rates and held UCPB liable under TILA (P26,000 penalty).
issue: Whether the one-sided interest-rate stipulation is valid, and whether UCPB violated the Truth in Lending Act by failing to disclose the true finance charges before consummation.
ruling: The Supreme Court AFFIRMED with modifications: (1) the interest-rate provision is void — it violates mutuality of contracts and TILA for not disclosing the true finance charges; only the 12% legal interest (compounded as stipulated) plus a reduced 12% penalty apply; (2) UCPB violated TILA — giving borrowers copies of the notes AFTER execution is not substantial compliance with the 'prior to consummation' rule; (3) the P26,000 Sec. 6(a) penalty stands and is deducted from the spouses' liability; (4) the foreclosure itself is VALID, with the recomputed amounts deducted from the foreclosure proceeds.
doctrine: TILA requires a clear written disclosure of the finance charge (pesos and centavos) and its simple-annual-rate equivalent BEFORE consummation; belated copies after execution do not substantially comply. A stipulation letting the lender unilaterally fix or increase interest violates TILA's full-disclosure policy and the Civil Code rule on mutuality, and is void. Sec. 6 creates BOTH a civil liability (6a: P100 or twice the finance charge, whichever greater, capped at P2,000 per transaction, 1-year prescription) recoverable separately and independently of the criminal liability for willful violation (6c); the civil cause of action accrues when the finance charge is required.
keyPhrase: Disclose before consummation; one-sided rates are void; civil and criminal liabilities are separate.
examUse: Use for: prior-disclosure timing, void escalation/one-sided rate clauses, Sec. 6(a) penalty formula and 1-year prescription/accrual, civil-vs-criminal distinction, and the P1,000 reading of the Sec. 6(c) fine floor.

name: New Sampaguita Builders Construction, Inc. and Spouses Eduardo R. Dee and Arcelita M. Dee v. Philippine National Bank
citation: G.R. No. 148753, 30 July 2004, 479 Phil. 483 (Third Division, Panganiban, J.)
facts: NSBCI obtained an P8M commercial loan from PNB (P7.7M revolving credit line + P0.3M unadvised line) via three promissory notes (P5M, P2.7M, P0.3M), secured by mortgages on the Dee spouses' properties. PNB unilaterally raised interest rates and penalties (penalty up to 36%) without the borrowers' consent; the increases appeared in statements of account but not in the disclosure statements. NSBCI sued over the bloated loan; the CA upheld PNB.
issue: Whether PNB may collect increased interest, penalties, and other charges that were not revealed in the disclosure statements, and whether courts may strike down one-sided escalation provisions.
ruling: The Supreme Court PARTLY GRANTED the petition: courts may strike down or modify note provisions giving lenders unrestrained power to raise rates without prior notice and consent; only the rates actually disclosed (19.5% and 21.5% effective) could be imposed; the unilaterally hiked 36% penalty was equitably reduced to zero as iniquitous; and PNB was ordered to refund P3,686,101.52 in overcollections with legal interest.
doctrine: Excessive interests, penalties, and other charges not revealed in disclosure statements issued by banks, even if stipulated in the promissory notes, cannot be given effect under the Truth in Lending Act. The borrower not clearly informed through the disclosure statement before consummation of the availment/drawdown cannot be made to pay such charges or increases. A disclosure statement is not a contract modifiable by a later promissory note — it is the written reflection of the true and effective cost of the loan, and novation is never presumed.
keyPhrase: Undisclosed charges cannot be collected even if the note stipulates them.
examUse: Use for: effect of nondisclosure on collectibility of charges, disclosure-statement-vs-promissory-note hierarchy, unilateral escalation without notice/consent, and equitable reduction of iniquitous penalties.
