name: Jaime N. Gapayao v. Rosario Fulo, SSS and SSC
facts: Jaime Fulo died in 1997 while doing repairs at Jaime Gapayao's residence and business establishment. His widow Rosario claimed SSS death benefits, but Fulo was not SSS-registered. She insisted he had been Gapayao's farm laborer, abaca harvester, and repairman/utility worker from 1983 to 1997. Gapayao denied employment, though he had earlier signed a Compromise Agreement describing himself as the 'employer' of the deceased and paying P40,000 as full settlement. The SSC found an employer-employee relationship and ordered Gapayao to pay unpaid contributions, penalties, and Sec. 24(a) damages; the CA affirmed.
issue: Whether Jaime Fulo was Gapayao's employee and therefore compulsorily covered by the Social Security Law.
ruling: Yes. The Supreme Court denied the petition and affirmed the CA. Applying the control test — the right to control the end and the manner and means, not necessarily its exercise — the Court held Gapayao controlled Fulo directly or through his farm overseer; pakyaw workers are employees while subject to control, and irregular hours or seasonal work do not negate employment. The Compromise Agreement's 'employer' admission was a declaration against interest.
doctrine: The right to SSS coverage is premised on the employer-employee relationship, determined by the control test (right to control suffices; delegation to an overseer counts). Pakyaw, seasonal, or irregular-hour workers are employees when controlled. SSC factual findings supported by substantial evidence and affirmed by the CA are final. An unreported worker's death triggers Sec. 24(a) damages against the employer.
keyPhrase: Coverage follows the employment relationship; control test decides who is an employee.
examUse: Use for any question asking whether a worker (pakyaw, seasonal, project-based, househelp-adjacent) is compulsorily covered, and for Sec. 24(a) failure-to-report damages.

name: Social Security System v. Rosanna H. Aguas, et al.
facts: Pablo Aguas, an SSS member-pensioner, died in 1996. His widow Rosanna claimed death benefits for herself and minor Jeylnn; the claim was initially paid, then suspended after Pablo's sister alleged Rosanna had long abandoned Pablo, lived with another man, and that the children were not Pablo's. Janet later joined as a third claimant. The SSC denied all claims and ordered a refund; the CA reversed and declared all three entitled. The evidence showed: Rosanna and Pablo had separated years before his death; Jeylnn's birth certificate (signed by Pablo as father, verified with the civil register) supported legitimacy; Janet's birth proof was an unverified photocopy and witnesses uniformly said she was merely informally 'adopted.'
issue: Whether Rosanna, Jeylnn, and Janet are entitled to the SSS death benefits as primary beneficiaries.
ruling: Only Jeylnn. The petition was partially granted and the CA ruling affirmed with modification: (1) Jeylnn is legitimate — children conceived or born during the marriage are presumed legitimate (Family Code Art. 164), and the SSS failed to overcome the presumption; (2) Janet is not a dependent child — her birth was not substantially proven and only 'legally adopted' children qualify; (3) Rosanna, though the legitimate spouse, failed to prove she was still dependent on Pablo for support at his death — dependency cannot be presumed from marriage alone, and a de facto separated spouse is presumed not dependent absent contrary proof.
doctrine: A claimant-spouse must establish two qualifying factors: (1) legitimate spouse, AND (2) dependent on the member for support at death. Dependency is proved, never presumed from marriage; separation breaks the presumption of support the other way. Only legitimate, legitimated, legally adopted, or illegitimate children within the statute qualify as dependent children — informal adoptees do not.
keyPhrase: Legitimate spouse AND dependent for support — two factors, both proved.
examUse: Use for every death-benefit beneficiary question: apply the two-factor spouse test and the closed-list child rule before distributing under Sec. 13 and Sec. 8(k).

name: Ibarra P. Ortega v. Social Security Commission and SSS
facts: Ortega, an SSS member, received partial permanent disability pension for 23 months for generalized arthritis and partial ankylosis. After it expired, he claimed total permanent disability benefits in 2000, invoking his private physicians' diagnoses (trigger finger, asthma, hypertension, GERD, rheumatoid arthritis). SSS medical officers repeatedly examined him and found no progression of illness (only slight limitation of grasping movement). The SSC denied the claim (and noted he could opt for retirement, having turned 60 with 41 contributions); the CA affirmed.
issue: Whether Ortega is entitled to total permanent disability benefits despite the SSS medical findings of no progression.
ruling: No. The Supreme Court denied the petition. The Court is not a trier of facts; SSC factual findings, affirmed by the CA and supported by substantial evidence (the SSS medical examinations), are final. The case also draws the conceptual line: Labor Code compensation (work-related disability, loss of income from work-connected injury/illness) and Social Security Law benefits (insurance against disability, sickness, old age, death, irrespective of work-connection) differ in nature and purpose — and 'total and permanent' means different things under each regime.
doctrine: Total permanent disability under the SSS Law is adjudicated on SSS medical findings under the substantial-evidence standard; courts defer to SSC expertise as affirmed by the CA. SSS benefits and Labor Code employees' compensation are distinct regimes — a Labor Code disability theory does not control an SSS disability claim.
keyPhrase: SSS disability is an insurance benefit judged on SSS medical findings, not a Labor Code compensation claim.
examUse: Use for disability questions to explain who decides (SSS/SSC on medical evidence), the standard (substantial evidence), and the SSS-vs-Labor-Code distinction.

name: Ambassador Hotel, Inc. v. Social Security System
facts: The SSS charged Ambassador Hotel's president Yolanda Chan and treasurer with violation of Secs. 22(a), 22(d), and 28(e) for non-remittance of contributions (June 1999-March 2001, assessed at P769,575.48 with penalties). At trial, Yolanda proved an intra-corporate dispute had prevented her from acting as president during the delinquency period. The RTC acquitted her criminally (she was not the 'managing head' under Sec. 28(f)) but held the hotel civilly liable for P584,804.00; the CA affirmed in toto. The hotel argued the RTC had no jurisdiction over it since it was never impleaded or served summons.
issue: Whether the corporation is civilly liable for unremitted SSS contributions despite its officer's criminal acquittal, and whether jurisdiction attached without separate summons.
ruling: Yes on both. The Supreme Court denied the petition: (1) SSS remittance is mandatory; a corporation cannot invoke separate personality to escape liability — Sec. 28(f) pins criminal responsibility on the managing head/directors/partners while the corporation answers civilly; (2) arrest of the managing head gives the court jurisdiction over the corporation (no separate summons needed; it is deemed included through its officers); jurisdiction once attached is not ousted by later acquittal; (3) the acquittal did not extinguish the civil action, which is deemed instituted with the criminal action and survives unless the judgment declares the underlying fact did not exist. The Court found by preponderance of evidence that P584,804.00 in contributions went unremitted, plus 6% legal interest.
doctrine: SSS contribution remittance is mandatory. Under Sec. 28(f), corporate officers bear personal criminal liability while the corporation bears civil liability; jurisdiction over the corporation attaches through its arrested officers; and an officer's acquittal does not extinguish corporate civil liability unless the judgment negates the fact of non-payment.
keyPhrase: Mandatory remittance; officers answer criminally, the corporation civilly — acquittal of one is not acquittal of the other.
examUse: Use for penalties and employer-liability questions: mandatory nature, Sec. 28(f) personal liability, jurisdiction, and the criminal/civil split.
note: Decided under RA 1161 as amended by RA 8282; the cited doctrines carry into identical RA 11199 provisions (Secs. 22, 28(e)-(f)). The 3%-per-month delinquency penalty discussed in the decision is the pre-2019 rate; RA 11199 Sec. 22(a) imposes 2% per month.
